prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

We smuggle crates of Beaujolais through the squeaky pantry door. We steal cases of cigarettes, borrow the bulletproof Mercedes to race through the capital’s empty streets. It’s wonderful, the peace. No local can afford a car, except the police. The police stand beside their cars and wave. The police lack petrol for their cars. There’s a beer bottle shortage in the nation. There are no bars. Drunk driving is a hobby. Driving while high is an art. No one in the bad girls’ group is not in the back of the Mercedes, Vijay on Ashanti drum all the way to the beach. Money is worthless. Cigarettes are money. We are thirteen. We rent a hut roofed with palm fronds. We lie out on the sand with our bottles of French wine and our Hong Kong blondes and look up at the Atlantic Slave Coast midnight sky:shine all my diamonds shine ’cause they really diamonds.

outputs.L1: We smuggle crates of Beaujolais through the squeaking pantry door. We steal cases of cigarettes and borrow the bulletproof Mercedes to race through the capital’s deserted streets. The peace is wonderful. No local can afford a car except the police, who stand beside theirs and wave; they have no petrol to drive them. There is a nationwide shortage of beer bottles. There are no bars. Drunk driving is a hobby; driving while high, an art. Every member of the bad girls’ group is packed into the back of the Mercedes, with Vijay playing the Ashanti drum all the way to the beach. Money is worthless. Cigarettes are currency. We are thirteen. We rent a hut roofed with palm fronds, then lie on the sand with our bottles of French wine and our Hong Kong blondes, gazing up at the midnight sky above the Atlantic Slave Coast: shine all my diamonds shine ’cause they really diamonds.
outputs.L2:
Through the pantry’s creaking entrance, we secretly haul boxes of Beaujolais. We pilfer cartons of cigarettes and take the armored Mercedes for joyrides along the deserted avenues of the capital. The calm is glorious. Apart from the police, residents cannot afford cars—and the officers, without fuel, merely stand by their vehicles and wave.

The country has run out of beer bottles, and bars do not exist. Driving drunk is a pastime; driving stoned is a craft. All thirteen members of the bad-girls crew cram into the Mercedes, with Vijay beating an Ashanti drum until we reach the beach. Cash has no value, so cigarettes serve as currency. We hire a palm-frond-roofed hut, stretch out on the sand beside our French wine and blond cigarettes from Hong Kong, and gaze at the midnight sky over the Atlantic Slave Coast, singing for our diamonds to sparkle because they are real.
outputs.L3:
The group survives through a mixture of smuggling, theft, and reckless adventure. They bring wine into the country illegally, steal cigarettes, and race a bulletproof Mercedes through the capital’s deserted streets. The emptiness reflects the widespread poverty and chronic shortages that have overtaken the city: most residents cannot afford cars, and even the police often have no petrol for their vehicles.

Social disorder has transformed everyday life. Bars have effectively disappeared, driving while drunk or under the influence of drugs has become commonplace, and cigarettes are so scarce that they are often considered more valuable than money. Against this chaotic backdrop, thirteen members of the “bad girls’ group” accompany Vijay to a beach on the Atlantic Slave Coast. There, they rent a simple palm-roofed hut and spend the night drinking wine, smoking, and lying beneath the open midnight sky.
outputs.L4:
The passage presents a group of expatriates celebrating their freedom in a country devastated by war and economic collapse. Told through a first-person catalogue of exploits, the narrative moves rapidly from smuggling and reckless driving to heavy drinking, bribery, and carefree recreation. The accumulating details create an atmosphere of exhilaration: ordinary restrictions seem to have disappeared, danger becomes entertainment, and institutional breakdown offers the outsiders opportunities unavailable in a stable society. Their ability to cross borders, obtain scarce goods, evade consequences, and move freely through the country marks them as unusually privileged.

Yet the excitement is inseparable from the suffering surrounding it. The beaches, alcohol, vehicles, and illicit commodities enjoyed by the expatriates exist alongside shortages, damaged infrastructure, weakened public institutions, and widespread poverty. What appears to them as openness or adventure is, for local people, the result of political violence and material deprivation. The outsiders can treat instability as temporary liberation because they possess money, mobility, foreign status, and the possibility of leaving. Local residents, by contrast, must endure the long-term consequences of the same conditions.

The first-person perspective intensifies this moral tension. By allowing the expatriates to recount their behavior casually, even proudly, the passage exposes their lack of self-awareness without necessarily offering direct judgment. The energetic list of pleasures initially invites the reader to share their sense of freedom, but its excess gradually becomes disturbing. Reckless driving and intoxication are not merely signs of youthful spontaneity; they demonstrate confidence that normal rules will not be enforced against them. Smuggling likewise suggests that the collapse of legal and economic systems has become a source of convenience and amusement for people insulated from its worst effects.

The beach celebration brings these contradictions into sharp focus. A beach may suggest peace, leisure, and escape, but here that peace is built within a landscape shaped by scarcity and institutional failure. The expatriates experience the nation as a space where they can live more intensely and cheaply than they could at home. Their freedom therefore depends on inequality: local hardship lowers prices, weakens regulation, and increases the power of foreign money and connections. Even their apparent rejection of conventional authority relies on another form of authority—the social and economic privilege attached to being outsiders.

Ultimately, the passage challenges romantic ideas about expatriate life in unstable or postwar societies. It shows that one group’s adventure can be another group’s crisis, and that “freedom” is not equally available to everyone. The outsiders’ celebration may feel peaceful and carefree, but it is sustained by conditions produced through war, deprivation, and longer histories of foreign intervention or exploitation. By juxtaposing pleasure with ruin, the passage reveals the ethical cost hidden beneath the expatriates’ exhilaration: they are not simply escaping disorder but benefiting from it.
outputs.L5: The sun dipped behind the vineyards of Beaujolais as a silver Mercedes followed the winding road through rows of autumn-colored vines. In the quiet villages, cafés prepared for an evening of music, conversation, and newly opened bottles. The journey felt timeless—a blend of French charm, elegant engineering, and the simple pleasure of discovering what waited beyond the next curve.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a vivid first-person plural prose poem about thirteen reckless expatriate teenagers partying in a poor West African capital, using stolen cigarettes, contraband Beaujolais, a bulletproof Mercedes, corrupt police, and a midnight beach scene.
counterfactuals.output:
We were thirteen expatriate children, reckless with borrowed countries, our parents’ passports sleeping in embassy drawers while we stole cigarettes from silver cases and smoked them badly beneath the slow, indifferent fans. The city sweated around us—tin roofs, generator coughs, gutters bright with rain—and we drank contraband Beaujolais from chipped tea glasses, laughing at the sourness as if laughter could make us older. We had money enough to misunderstand everything.

At eleven we crowded into the bulletproof Mercedes, thirteen knees, thirteen mouths, perfume and tobacco and red wine breathing together behind darkened glass. The driver had gone home, so one of us drove, too fast, through streets where kerosene lamps trembled beside pyramids of oranges. At the checkpoint, the police raised a hand. Their uniforms were faded at the seams; their rifles looked tired. We folded bills beneath a foreign driver’s license. The officer’s face hardened, softened, vanished in our rearview mirror. We cheered as though corruption were a gate we had invented.

By midnight we reached the beach. The Atlantic came black and enormous, breaking its white teeth against the sand. We kicked off our shoes and ran toward it, thirteen pale comets under a bruised moon, passing fishermen’s canoes drawn above the tide line, passing cooking fires gone to embers, passing the sleeping city’s last small lights. Someone carried the bottle; someone carried the cigarettes; someone climbed onto the Mercedes hood and declared us immortal.

But the ocean would not applaud. It seized our ankles and dragged at us with the cold strength of consequence. For one breath we stood silent, shoulder to shoulder, listening to the surf erase our names. Behind us the armored car gleamed like a sealed confession. Ahead, the dark water kept arriving. We drank, we smoked, we shouted into it—all thirteen of us young enough to believe the night belonged to us, and old enough, almost, to know it never had.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a darkly comic literary passage set during political unrest, where privileged young people race through deserted streets, treat cigarettes as currency, and celebrate on the Atlantic coast. Use short, rhythmic sentences and end with a lyrical line about diamonds.
counterfactuals.output:
The ministers fled at noon.

By dusk, the sons of ministers had stolen their cars.

They raced through the emptied avenues. Past smashed kiosks. Past statues wearing traffic cones. Past the parliament, which smoldered with bureaucratic patience.

Luc drove a silver coupé. Ana stood through the sunroof and waved a dead flag. Tomas fired a champagne cork at a police drone.

Nobody arrested them.

Nobody was left.

Cigarettes had become money. One for bread. Two for petrol. Five for a rumor about the border. They carried cartons under their coats and tipped the frightened like emperors.

At midnight they reached the Atlantic.

The hotel had no staff, so they appointed themselves staff. They raided the cellar. They dragged white sofas onto the beach. They toasted the revolution, though none could agree who had started it.

Behind them, the country changed hands.

Before them, the black water applauded.

They danced until morning, rich, ridiculous, and briefly immortal, while the last fires inland glittered like diamonds the earth had coughed up for the sea.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a decadent coming-of-age vignette in the style of fragmented memoir. Include a squeaky pantry door, cases of cigarettes, petrol-starved police, an Ashanti drum, French wine, “Hong Kong blondes,” and a palm-frond hut on the beach.
counterfactuals.output:
The pantry door squeaked all through that summer, a thin, guilty sound, though no one in the house seemed capable of guilt. Behind it: tins of peaches, powdered milk, ant colonies, and cases of cigarettes stacked to the ceiling—American brands with white filters, English brands in severe red packets, “Hong Kong blondes” in gold cartons that made us cough and feel cosmopolitan.

I was seventeen and had begun lying beautifully.

*

The police had no petrol.

Their Land Rovers stood outside the station beneath a jacaranda tree, blue lamps dusty, tyres slowly softening. If trouble happened, they arrived on bicycles or not at all. This gave the town an atmosphere of provisional freedom. Curfew was announced, ignored, announced again.

At night we drove without headlights.

At dawn we swore we had been asleep.

*

A Frenchman named Luc kept wine beneath his bed. It was French wine because he said so, though the labels had peeled off in the humidity and the bottles tasted of vinegar, iron, and roses left too long in a vase.

We drank it from enamel cups.

Someone beat an Ashanti drum in the courtyard—a dark, taut instrument with a voice larger than the boy who played it. The rhythm entered my ribs and rearranged them. I danced barefoot with Sabine, who had cut her hair with kitchen scissors and wore a silk slip the color of bruised plums.

“You’re still a child,” she told me.

Then she kissed me as if to prove otherwise.

*

There were coins in the sand, teeth in the smiles, salt on every surface.

The sea had the vulgar blue of a postcard.

We built a palm-frond hut on the beach and called it the Republic. Its laws were simple: no surnames, no clocks, no confessions before midnight. We furnished it with a torn mattress, two hurricane lamps, six bottles of wine, and an ashtray made from a sardine tin.

By the end of the week the roof leaked.

By the end of the month everyone had betrayed everyone else.

*

I remember the Hong Kong blondes passing from hand to hand, their smoke sweet and chemical. I remember Luc asleep with his cheek against the drum. I remember Sabine walking into the surf still dressed, her slip opening around her like ink.

I remember believing decadence meant abundance.

It did not.

It meant using everything up before someone came to take it away.

*

The pantry door squeaked the night my father found us stealing the last case of cigarettes. He stood in the yellow passage light, barefoot, diminished by fever and unpaid bills.

“Take them,” he said. “Take the damned things.”

That was the moment, though I did not know it then.

Not the kisses. Not the wine. Not the police pushing their empty vehicles down the road while we laughed from the verandah. Not the drum or the hut or the sea.

It was my father turning away, and the door continuing to complain behind him.

*

Years later, I would search for that beach and find a hotel where the palms had been. The town had petrol now. The police cars flashed blue along the paved road. No one remembered Luc. No one admitted to knowing Sabine.

In the hotel bar I ordered French wine.

It arrived cold, correct, and without mystery.

I drank alone, listening for a drum beneath the music, for the small hinge-cry of the pantry door, for the sound of seventeen slipping out through a house that could no longer afford to keep it.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Turn the following scenario into tense, sensory present-tense narration from a collective “we” perspective: a group called the bad girls borrows a bulletproof Mercedes, drives drunk through an impoverished capital, and spends the night drinking beneath the Slave Coast sky.
counterfactuals.output:
We call ourselves the bad girls because nobody else gets to name us.

The Mercedes is borrowed, black, bulletproof, heavy as a secret. Its doors shut with the blunt thud of a vault. Inside, the leather smells of heat, perfume, and somebody else’s money. We pass the bottle between us. Liquor scorches our throats; laughter rattles against the dark windows.

We drive too fast through the capital.

Night crowds the windshield. Potholes lunge from the road. Market fires gutter beneath patched umbrellas, and barefoot children flash silver in the headlights before vanishing into alleys. Diesel smoke coats our tongues. Open drains breathe rot. Motorbikes swarm, horns shriek, and every hard turn sends us sliding shoulder to shoulder while the Mercedes shoulders on, armored and indifferent.

We know we are drunk. We know the city is awake around us, hungry and watching. Our hands clench the seats when the tires skid. For one breathless second, the car drifts toward a roadside stall, toward a woman lifting both arms—and then the wheel jerks, bottles topple, glass knocks glass, and we tear past with our hearts battering our ribs.

By the time we reach the coast, the night wind is wet with salt.

We park beneath a sky once mapped by slavers, a vast black bowl pricked with cold stars. The sea keeps coming, wave after wave, dragging chains of foam across the sand. We sit on the hood and drink until the metal cools beneath our thighs. Behind us, the capital flickers and growls. Before us, the Slave Coast breathes in the dark.

We do not feel bulletproof now.

We feel the bottle growing lighter. We feel sand between our teeth, salt drying on our skin, history pressing close as another body. We lean into one another and listen to the surf erase our names, then give them back.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a 150-word piece of experimental travel fiction contrasting expatriate excess with local scarcity in a nation where money is worthless, beer bottles are scarce, there are no bars, and almost nobody can afford a car.
counterfactuals.output:
I arrived with a suitcase of dollars, crisp as autumn leaves, and discovered they bought less than leaves. At the hotel, expatriates staged abundance: perfume, imported olives, gin poured into teacups because beer bottles had become treasure. Outside, the capital clicked its tongue at us. Rickshaws outnumbered cars; a private sedan passed like a comet, witnessed and immediately mythologized. There were no bars, only apartments with curtains drawn, where foreigners traded hard currency for warm lager and called it hardship.

Mara, a teacher, carried one empty bottle three districts to exchange for cooking oil. I followed, useless pockets whispering paper, paper. At the market, prices changed between question and answer. A child folded a banknote into a bird; it flew farther than wages.

That night, upstairs, corks popped. Below, neighbors queued for bread beneath a dead streetlamp. The city swallowed our music, then returned one sound: glass clinking, empty, precious, unbroken.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
